A Florida enhanced life estate deed, usually called a lady bird deed, lets the grantor keep a life estate and control of the property while naming who receives it later. This guide uses a clerk-published form and the Florida Constitution's homestead rules. We could not confirm a statute that names this deed type.

What the clerk form says

  • An enhanced life estate (lady bird) deed form recorded with the St. Lucie County Clerk states: 'The Grantor reserves a life estate for himself/herself during the Grantor's lifetime coupled with an unrestricted power to convey during the Grantor's lifetime, which includes the power to sell, gift, mortgage, lease and otherwise dispose of the property, and to retain the proceeds from the conveyance.' (St. Lucie County Clerk of Court, Enhanced Life Estate Deed (Lady Bird Deed) form).

Homestead rules that apply

  • The homestead shall not be subject to devise if the owner is survived by a spouse or a minor child or children, except that the homestead may be devised to the owner's spouse if there is no minor child. 'Devise' includes a disposition by trust of the portion of the trust estate that would be the grantor's homestead. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 732.4015(1)-(2))
  • If not devised as authorized, homestead descends as other intestate property, except that if the decedent is survived by a spouse and descendants, the spouse takes a life estate with a vested remainder to the descendants per stirpes. This section does not apply to property owned in tenancy by the entireties or joint tenancy with right of survivorship. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 732.401(1), (5))

What is a lady bird deed in Florida?

An enhanced life estate deed. The grantor reserves a life estate for themselves and, on the form we reviewed, keeps control of the property during life.

Does homestead status limit who can inherit?

Yes. Homestead cannot be devised if the owner is survived by a spouse or minor child, with limited exceptions (Const. art. X, Sec. 4).

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Florida requires 7 years of actual continued possession under a claim of title for adverse possession without color of title, and an owner can ask the county sheriff for removal of people unlawfully occupying a home under Sec. 82.036. The statute text is verified; we could not confirm every procedural detail on official forms.

Adverse possession rules

  • Adverse possession under color of title requires entry under a claim of title founded on a written instrument, decree or judgment and continued possession for 7 years; the instrument must be recorded in the office of the clerk of the circuit court of the county for possession commencing after Dec. 31, 1945. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 95.16(1))
  • Adverse possession without color of title requires 7 years of actual continued possession under a claim of title exclusive of any other right, and the claimant must pay all outstanding taxes and matured special improvement liens within 1 year after entering possession, file a return with the property appraiser within 30 days after complying, and pay taxes for all remaining years. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 95.18(1))
  • The return to the property appraiser must carry a notarized attestation and a description of use, and must state in 12-point uppercase boldface: THIS RETURN DOES NOT CREATE ANY INTEREST ENFORCEABLE BY LAW IN THE DESCRIBED PROPERTY. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 95.18(3))
  • Upon a return, the property appraiser mails a copy to the owner of record, informs the owner that tax payments by the owner before April 1 following the assessment year have priority, and notes the tax roll that an adverse possession claim has been submitted. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 95.18(4))
  • A person who occupies or attempts to occupy a residential structure solely by claim of adverse possession before making the required return commits trespass under s. 810.08; one who also offers the property for lease commits theft under s. 812.014. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 95.18(9)-(10))

Sheriff removal under Sec. 82.036

  • Sec. 82.036 lets a property owner or authorized agent ask the county sheriff for immediate removal of persons unlawfully occupying a residential dwelling if: the requester is the owner/agent; the property is a residential dwelling; the occupants entered unlawfully and remain; the property was not open to the public at entry; the owner has directed them to leave; they are not current or former tenants under a rental agreement; they are not immediate family; and there is no pending litigation between owner and occupant. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 82.036(2))
  • The owner submits a verified Complaint to Remove Persons Unlawfully Occupying Residential Real Property, under penalty of perjury, with a copy of government-issued ID (or agent authority documents). The sheriff verifies the owner is the record owner or agent, then 'without delay' serves a notice to immediately vacate and puts the owner in possession; service may be by hand or posting on the front door. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 82.036(3)-(4))
  • The sheriff is entitled to the same fee as for serving a writ of possession under s. 30.231; if the owner requests a standby to keep the peace while changing locks and moving personal property to or near the property line, the sheriff may charge a reasonable hourly rate. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 82.036(5))
  • A person harmed by wrongful removal under Sec. 82.036 may be restored to possession and may recover actual costs and damages, statutory damages equal to triple the fair market rent of the dwelling, court costs and reasonable attorney fees. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 82.036(6))
  • Sec. 82.036 history notes: s. 1, ch. 2024-44; s. 1, ch. 2025-112; s. 9, ch. 2026-14 (the 2024 enactment is the HB 621 law; the HB number itself was not verified on the statute page). (Fla. Stat. Sec. 82.036 History note)

What we could not confirm

  • Whether the 2024 law was effective July 1, 2024 not confirmed from an opened page.
  • That ch. 2024-44 was House Bill 621 was not confirmed on an official page opened in this session.

Florida Squatters Rights FAQ

How long does adverse possession take in Florida?

Without color of title it requires 7 years of actual continued possession under a claim of title, and the claimant must also meet the property tax return rules in Ch. 95.

Can I ask the sheriff to remove squatters?

Sec. 82.036 lets an owner or agent ask the county sheriff for immediate removal of persons unlawfully occupying a residential dwelling, using a verified complaint.

What if the sheriff removes the wrong person?

A person harmed by wrongful removal may be restored to possession and recover costs and damages (Sec. 82.036).

Last updated November 14, 2026.

A Florida landlord can end a tenancy for unpaid rent with a written 3-day notice that excludes weekends and legal holidays, and must go to county court to recover possession. Landlords cannot lock tenants out. This guide summarizes Chapter 83 as the Florida Statutes show it.

Notices

  • If a tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday and legal holidays (court-observed only), after delivery of written demand for payment or possession, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 83.56(3))
  • For noncompliance a tenant should not be given a chance to cure (for example intentional destruction of property), the landlord may terminate and the tenant has 7 days from delivery of the notice to vacate. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 83.56(2)(a))
  • For curable noncompliance (for example unauthorized pets, guests or vehicles), the landlord delivers a written notice giving 7 days from delivery to correct it, or the lease is deemed terminated; if the same conduct recurs within 12 months the tenancy is subject to termination without further warning. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 83.56(2)(b))
  • Written notices may be delivered by mailing, delivering a true copy, e-mailing per s. 83.505, or, if the tenant is absent, leaving a copy at the residence; the notice requirements may not be waived in the rental agreement. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 83.56(4))
  • A landlord who accepts partial rent after posting a nonpayment notice must give a receipt stating date, amount and balance, or place the partial rent in the court registry upon filing, or post a new 3-day notice. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 83.56(5)(a))

Get My Cash Offer →

Court process

  • To recover possession after termination, the landlord, attorney or agent files a complaint in the county court of the county where the premises are located; an agent who is not an attorney may only do the initial filing. The landlord is entitled to the summary procedure of s. 51.011. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 83.59(2))
  • A landlord may recover possession only through an action for possession or other civil action determining the right of possession, on surrender, on abandonment, or when the last remaining tenant has died, property remains, rent is unpaid, at least 60 days have passed and no probate estate notice has been given. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 83.59(3))
  • If the tenant raises any defense other than payment, the tenant must pay the accrued rent and rent accruing during the case into the court registry, or file a motion to determine rent, within 5 days (excluding Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays) after service of process; failure is an absolute waiver of defenses other than payment and the landlord gets an immediate default judgment and writ of possession. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 83.60(2))

Ending tenancies and costs

  • A tenancy without a specific term may be ended by written notice: year to year, not less than 60 days before the end of the annual period; quarter to quarter, 30 days; month to month, 30 days; week to week, 7 days. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 83.57(1)-(4))
  • The prevailing party in a possession action is entitled to judgment for costs and execution. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 83.59(4))

What we could not confirm

  • County court filing fees not confirmed.
  • Sheriff writ of possession timing (24 hours notice, s. 83.62) not opened.
  • Statute history shows s. 83.56 amended by ch. 2026-143; effective date and substance of that change were not verified.

Florida Eviction Process FAQ

How much notice does a Florida landlord give for unpaid rent?

A written notice demanding payment or possession within 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday and legal holidays (Sec. 83.56).

Where is an eviction filed?

In the county court of the county where the premises are located.

Can a landlord change the locks to remove a tenant?

No. Possession is recovered only through court action, surrender or abandonment (Sec. 83.59).

  • Two years after a person's death, neither the estate, the personal representative nor the beneficiaries are liable for any claim against the decedent, whether or not letters were issued, except as provided in the section (a recorded mortgage or lien is not affected). A Florida deed must be signed in the presence of two subscribing witnesses (Sec. 689.01), and the clerk will record it only if it carries printed names and post-office addresses. Documentary stamp tax on deeds is 70 cents per $100 of consideration.

Signing and recording

  • No estate of freehold, or for a term of more than 1 year, may be created, granted, transferred or released other than by a written instrument signed in the presence of two subscribing witnesses by the grantor or the grantor's lawfully authorized agent (no witnesses required for a lease). No seal is necessary. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 689.01(1))
  • The two-witness requirement may be satisfied by witnesses present and electronically signing by audio-video communication technology as defined in s. 117.201. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 689.01(2)(a))
  • To be recorded by the circuit court clerk, the instrument must show the printed name and post-office address of each signer, the preparer's name and address, each witness' printed name and address, the notary's printed name, and each grantee's name and address. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 695.26(1))
  • The first page must reserve a 3-inch by 3-inch space at the top right corner (and 1-inch by 3-inch on each subsequent page) for the clerk's use. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 695.26(1)(e))

Doc stamp tax

  • Documentary stamp tax on deeds is 70 cents on each $100 (or fractional part) of consideration, and consideration includes money paid, discharge of an obligation, and the amount of any mortgage or other encumbrance, whether or not assumed. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 201.02(1)(a))
  • If the consideration includes property other than money, it is presumed equal to the fair market value of the real property. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 201.02(1)(a))

  • Florida does not statutorily define 'warranty deed' beyond common law; not confirmed.

Two subscribing witnesses (Sec. 689.01). Witnesses may sign electronically by audio-video technology as the statute defines.

What is the doc stamp tax on a Florida deed?

When a Florida owner dies without a valid will, the surviving spouse takes the entire intestate estate if the decedent left no descendants, and shares change when descendants exist. Undevised homestead follows its own rule.

Spouse and descendants

  • The surviving spouse's intestate share is the entire intestate estate if there is no surviving descendant of the decedent. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 732.102(1))
  • The spouse takes the entire intestate estate if all the decedent's descendants are also descendants of the spouse and the spouse has no other descendants. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 732.102(2))
  • If any surviving descendant of the decedent is not a lineal descendant of the surviving spouse, the spouse takes one-half of the intestate estate. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 732.102(3))
  • If all the decedent's descendants are also the spouse's, but the spouse has descendants who are not the decedent's, the spouse takes one-half of the intestate estate. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 732.102(4))

Chapter 732 sets shares for the spouse and descendants first, then parents, siblings and further relatives.

Deadlines and notices

  • Creditors must file claims on or before the later of 3 months after first publication of the notice to creditors or, for creditors required to be served, 30 days after service; claims not timely filed are barred even if no objection is filed, unless the court extends time for fraud, estoppel or insufficient notice.   • The personal representative must promptly serve the notice of administration on the surviving spouse, beneficiaries, and certain trustees and persons who may claim exempt property. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 733.212(1))
  • Objections to the validity of the will, venue or jurisdiction must be filed within 3 months after service of the notice of administration, extendable only for estoppel from a misstatement by the personal representative; in all events no later than the earlier of final discharge or 1 year after service. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 733.212(2)(c), (3))
  • A petition for determination of exempt property is due by the later of 4 months after service of the notice of administration or 40 days after termination of a will contest or related proceeding. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 733.212(2)(d))
  • An election to take the elective share must be filed by the earlier of 6 months after service of the notice of administration on the surviving spouse or 2 years after death, unless extended under s. 732.2135(2). (Fla. Stat. Sec. 733.212(2)(e))

Florida homestead is exempt from forced sale under court process, and it cannot be devised if the owner is survived by a spouse or minor child, with limited exceptions. A spouse who must join the deed has specific waiver language under Sec. 732.702.

Forced sale and devise limits

  • Homestead is exempt from forced sale under court process, with no judgment, decree or execution a lien on it, except for taxes and assessments, obligations contracted for purchase, improvement or repair, or labor performed on the realty; protected area is 160 contiguous acres outside a municipality or one-half acre within a municipality, plus personal property to the value of $1,000. (Fla. Const. Art. X Sec. 4(a))
  • The homestead shall not be subject to devise if the owner is survived by a spouse or minor child, except the homestead may be devised to the owner's spouse if there is no minor child. (Fla. Const. Art. X Sec. 4(c); Fla. Stat. Sec. 732.4015(1))
  • For this purpose a trust disposition counts as a devise: 'Devise' includes a disposition by trust of the portion of the trust estate that would be the grantor's homestead. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 732.4015(2)(b))

Spouse waivers and descent

  • A spouse waives surviving-spouse devise-restriction rights if the deed includes language substantially like: 'By executing or joining this deed, I intend to waive homestead rights that would otherwise prevent my spouse from devising the homestead property described in this deed to someone other than me.' (Fla. Stat. Sec. 732.7025(1)).
  • That waiver language is not a waiver of the protection against creditor claims, and not a waiver of the restriction against alienation by mortgage, sale, gift or deed without the joinder of the owner's spouse. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 732.7025(2))
  • If homestead is not devised, it descends as intestate property; with a spouse and descendants the spouse takes a life estate with a vested remainder in the descendants, or may elect within 6 months a one-half tenancy in common interest by recording a notice. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 732.401(1)-(2))

Divorce and spouses

  • In a divorce, the court sets apart nonmarital assets and, in distributing marital assets, 'must begin with the premise that the distribution should be equal, unless there is a justification for an unequal distribution based on all relevant factors'; one factor is retaining the marital home for a dependent child when equitable and financially feasible. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 61.075(1), (1)(h))
  • Marital assets include assets acquired during the marriage and the paydown of principal on a note and mortgage secured by nonmarital real property from marital funds; real property held as tenants by the entireties is presumed marital. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 61.075(6)(a))
  • An interspousal gift of real property requires a writing that complies with s. 689.01; a spouse joining a deed solely to convey homestead to someone other than the other spouse does not change the property's character to marital. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 61.075(6)(a)1.d)
  • Doc stamp tax does not apply to a deed between spouses or former spouses pursuant to a dissolution of marriage where the property is the marital home. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 201.02(7)(a))

What we could not confirm

  • Medicaid and creditor protection beyond the constitution not opened.
  • Whether a lady bird deed or trust avoids the devise restriction for homestead was not confirmed from an official source.
  • Subsection numbering for 61.075 items is taken from the extracted text; verify on the live page before citing a pinpoint.

Florida Homestead Protection FAQ

Is Florida homestead protected from creditors?

Yes, from forced sale under court process, with exceptions for taxes and assessments, purchase or improvement obligations, and labor on the property (Const. art. X, Sec. 4).

Can a spouse waive homestead devise rights?

Yes, by language in a deed or other writing that substantially tracks Sec. 732.702. It does not waive creditor protection or the restriction on alienation.

Does a spouse have to sign a deed on homestead?

Whether a spouse must join the deed depends on your facts, so ask a title company or Florida attorney. The statute we reviewed says a spouse joining a deed solely to convey homestead does not make the property marital (Sec. 61.075).

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Florida foreclosures go through court: after final judgment the clerk sells the property at public auction, generally 20 to 35 days later, and the owner can redeem until the clerk files the certificate of sale. This guide covers what Chapters 45 and 702 say; we did not confirm pre-suit notices or mediation programs.

The sale

  • In the order or final judgment of foreclosure the court directs the clerk to sell the property at public sale on a specified day not less than 20 days nor more than 35 days after the judgment (a later sale is allowed if the plaintiff consents). (Fla. Stat. Sec. 45.031(1)(a))
  • Notice of sale must be published on a publicly accessible website under s. 50.0311 for at least 2 consecutive weeks before the sale, or once a week for 2 consecutive weeks in a newspaper (second newspaper publication at least 5 days before the sale). (Fla. Stat. Sec. 45.031(2))
  • At the sale the successful high bidder posts a deposit equal to 5 percent of the final bid with the clerk; if final payment is not made in the prescribed period the clerk readvertises and pays costs from the deposit. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 45.031(3))
  • If no objections to the sale are filed within 10 days after the certificate of sale is filed, the clerk files a certificate of title; when it is filed the sale stands confirmed and title passes to the purchaser without further proceedings, and the clerk records it. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 45.031(5)-(6))

Redemption, deficiency and surplus

  • Right of redemption: at any time before the later of the clerk's filing of the certificate of sale or the time specified in the foreclosure judgment, the mortgagor or a subordinate interest holder may cure the debt and stop the sale by paying the amount in the judgment (or tendering performance due plus reasonable expenses and attorney's fees). 'Otherwise, there is no right of redemption.' (Fla. Stat. Sec. 45.0315).
  • Deficiency: entry of a deficiency decree is within the court's discretion, but for owner-occupied residential property the deficiency may not exceed the difference between the judgment amount (or outstanding debt in a short sale) and the fair market value on the date of sale. A property that had a homestead exemption on the latest certified roll before the foreclosure filing is rebuttably presumed owner-occupied. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 702.06)
  • Surplus funds: the final judgment must warn that subordinate lienholders must file a claim no later than the date the clerk reports the funds as unclaimed; homestead-exempt owners are told to check with the clerk within 10 days after the sale. After funds are reported unclaimed, only the owner of record as of the lis pendens date may claim the surplus. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 45.031(1)(a)-(b), (7)(b))

After the sale

  • Any party may object to the amount of the bid within 10 days after the certificate of sale is filed; the bid is conclusively presumed sufficient consideration, and the bid may be considered in setting any deficiency. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 45.031(8))
  • Finality of foreclosure judgment: if the challenger was properly served, appeal periods have run, and the property was acquired for value by an unaffiliated person with no lis pendens of record, a challenge to the judgment is treated solely as a claim for monetary damages and cannot adversely affect title. (History: s. 4, ch. 2013-137; s. 3, ch. 2023-215.) (Fla. Stat. Sec. 702.036(2)(a)).
  • If a party seeking relief from a foreclosure judgment claims a lien superior to the foreclosed lien, the court must award reasonable attorney fees to the prevailing party on that claim. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 702.036(5))
  • On a lienholder's request the court may issue an order to show cause for final judgment; the hearing may not occur sooner than the later of 20 days after service of the order or 45 days after service of the initial complaint (30 days after first publication if served by publication); the mortgage payment-during-foreclosure provision does not apply to an owner-occupied residence. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 702.10)
  • Doc stamp tax on the clerk's certificate of title in a foreclosure sale is computed on the highest and best bid. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 201.02(9))

What we could not confirm

  • Pre-suit notice requirements and mediation programs.
  • Pre-suit notice (paragraph 22 notice) and mediation programs not opened.
  • Writ of possession after certificate of title (s. 45.031 is silent; s. 83.62 not opened).

Florida Foreclosure Process FAQ

How long after judgment is a Florida foreclosure sale?

The court directs a sale on a specified day not less than 20 nor more than 35 days after the judgment, with exceptions (Sec. 45.031).

Can I stop the sale?

The owner can redeem by paying the debt before the later of the clerk filing the certificate of sale or the time in the judgment (Sec. 45.0315).

Can the lender seek a deficiency?

A deficiency decree is discretionary, and for owner-occupied residential property it is capped as Sec. 702.06 states.

Can I sell before the auction?

Yes. A sale that closes before the auction can pay off the loan from the proceeds, and any equity left is yours.

Documentary stamp tax

  • Documentary stamp tax on deeds is 70 cents on each $100 of consideration, and consideration includes the amount of any mortgage or other encumbrance, whether or not assumed. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 201.02(1)(a))
  • On promissory notes and written obligations to pay money, and on mortgages recorded in Florida, the tax is 35 cents on each $100 or fraction thereof of the indebtedness. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 201.08(1)(a)-(b))
  • The tax on a note under s. 201.08(1)(a) may not exceed $2,450; when there is both a mortgage and a note, the tax is paid on the mortgage at recording, and the statute states no such cap for the mortgage tax under paragraph (1)(b) in the text opened. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 201.08(1)(a)-(b))
  • A certificate of title issued by the clerk in a foreclosure judicial sale is subject to documentary stamp tax computed solely on the highest and best bid. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 201.02(9))
  • For a short sale, the taxable consideration does not include unpaid indebtedness forgiven or released by the mortgagee, if the grantor's mortgage debt exceeds consideration and the mortgagee is unrelated and receives no interest in the property. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 201.02(11))

  • The Financial Services Commission must adopt by rule the title insurance premium to be charged; rates may not be excessive, inadequate or unfairly discriminatory; the premium applies to each $100 of insurance; rates apply statewide and must be reviewed at least once every 3 years.   • If a discount period ends on a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday, it extends to the next working day if payment is delivered to the collector's designated office. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 197.162(4))

Federal exclusion rules

  • If you have a capital gain from the sale of your main home, you may qualify to exclude up to $250,000 of that gain from income, or up to $500,000 if you file a joint return with your spouse. (IRS Topic No. 701, Sale of Your Home)
  • Ownership test: you or your spouse owned the home for at least 24 months (2 years) out of the last 5 years before the sale. Use test: you used it as a residence for at least 24 months of the previous 5 years. (IRS Topic No. 701)
  • Generally you are not eligible for the exclusion if you excluded the gain from the sale of another home during the two-year period before the sale of your home. (IRS Topic No. 701)
  • If you receive Form 1099-S, you must report the sale even if the gain is excludable; you must also report it if you cannot exclude all the gain, using Schedule D (Form 1040) and Form 8949. (IRS Topic No. 701)
  • Publication 523 (2025): 'you may exclude the first $250,000 of gain from the sale of your home... The exclusion is increased to $500,000 for a married couple filing jointly.' (IRS Pub. 523 (2025), Selling Your Home).
  • A surviving spouse may take the higher exclusion if, among other conditions, the home is sold within 2 years of the death of the spouse. (IRS Pub. 523 (2025))
  • A reduced maximum exclusion may apply if the sale is due to a change in workplace location, a health issue, or an unforeseeable event. (IRS Pub. 523 (2025))

In Florida the clerk of the circuit court is the recorder of deeds, mortgages, liens and other instruments, and those Official Records stay open to public inspection. Recording a conveyance protects against later purchasers and creditors.

The clerk and the records

  • The clerk of the circuit court is the recorder of all instruments the clerk is required or authorized by law to record in the county, and records all instruments in one general series called 'Official Records'. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 28.222(1)-(2))
  • The clerk keeps a register with the filing number, date and hour of filing, kind of instrument and names of parties, and maintains a general alphabetical index, direct and inverse. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 28.222(2))
  • Deeds, leases, mortgages, claims of lien, satisfactions, lis pendens notices and judgments are among instruments the clerk records. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 28.222(3))
  • Instruments recorded in the Official Records must remain open to the public for inspection and copying; the clerk need not perform services without the service charges in s. 28.24. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 28.222(7))

Recording rules and fees

  • No conveyance, transfer or mortgage of real property (or lease of 1 year or longer) is good against creditors or subsequent purchasers for valuable consideration without notice unless recorded according to law. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 695.01(1))
  • Grantees by quitclaim are deemed bona fide purchasers without notice within the meaning of the recording acts. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 695.01(2))
  • A governmental lien for an improvement, service, fine or penalty (other than taxes, non-ad valorem or special assessments, or utilities) is valid against creditors and subsequent purchasers only if recorded in the county official records. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 695.01(3))
  • Recording fee for an instrument not more than 14 inches by 8.5 inches: first page or fraction $5.00; each additional page $4.00 (plus any other charges the clerk imposes; this is the s. 28.24(13) line). (Fla. Stat. Sec. 28.24(13))
  • To be recorded, an instrument must include printed names and addresses and reserve a 3 inch by 3 inch space on the first page for the clerk. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 695.26(1))

  • County clerk online search portals were not opened.
  • Time limit for marketable record title (Ch. 712, 30 years) not opened.
  • Additional recording surcharges (for example $1 per page historical preservation and $4 per page courts under s. 28.24 or ss. 28.2221, 201.15) were not opened.

The clerk of the circuit court, as recorder (Sec. 28.222).

What does recording cost?

For an instrument up to 14 by 8.5 inches the fee is $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 for each additional page, plus other charges (Sec. 28.24).

When a Florida rental property is sold, all security deposits and advance rents held for tenants must be transferred to the new owner or the buyer must be told to assume them. A landlord cannot use self-help to remove a tenant.

Sale and deposits

  • Upon the sale or transfer of title of rental property, all security deposits and advance rents held for tenants must be transferred to the new owner or agent with earned interest and an accounting of each tenant account; on transmittal of a written receipt the transferor is released from the holding obligation. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 83.49(7))
  • There is a rebuttable presumption that a new owner or agent received the security deposit from the previous owner; the presumption is limited to 1 month's rent. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 83.49(7))
  • If the landlord does not intend to claim the security deposit, it must be returned within 15 days after termination of the rental agreement; if the landlord intends a claim, written notice by certified mail or e-mail must be given within 30 days; failing that the landlord forfeits the right to set off against the deposit. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 83.49(3)(a))
  • The tenant has 15 days after receipt of the landlord's claim notice to object; if no objection, the landlord may deduct the claim and remit the balance within 30 days after the date of the notice. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 83.49(3)(b))
  • A deposit held must be in a separate non-interest-bearing or interest-bearing Florida account, or a surety bond posted (the lesser of the total deposits or $50,000 with the clerk); interest elections are at least 75 percent of the annualized average rate or 5 percent per year simple interest. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 83.49(1))
  • A renewal of an existing rental agreement is considered a new rental agreement and any deposit carried forward is a new security deposit. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 83.49(6))

Notice and possession

  • A tenancy without a specific term requires written notice to end it: 60 days (year to year), 30 days (quarter and month to month), 7 days (week to week). (Fla. Stat. Sec. 83.57)
  • A landlord cannot self-help evict; recovery of possession is only through court action, surrender, or abandonment (or the deceased last tenant provision). (Fla. Stat. Sec. 83.59(3))

What we could not confirm

  • Changes made by ch. 2026-143 to Sec. 83.56.
  • Notice-to-tenant requirements for showings (s. 83.53 access, 12 hours) not opened.
  • Whether a lease survives a sale (tenant protection after foreclosure, s. 83.561 and federal law) not opened.

Selling a Rented House in Florida FAQ

What happens to security deposits when I sell?

They must be transferred to the new owner or the new owner assumes them, as Sec. 83.49 provides.

Can I end a month-to-month tenancy to sell?

With written notice: 30 days for month to month, and 60 days year to year (Sec. 83.57).

A Florida construction lien does not continue longer than 1 year after the claim of lien is recorded unless suit is filed, and a claim must be recorded within 90 days after the lienor's final furnishing. An owner can shorten the time with a Notice of Contest of Lien.

Lien deadlines

  • A lien under the construction lien law does not continue for longer than 1 year after the claim of lien is recorded (or 1 year after an amended claim showing a later final furnishing date), unless within that time an action to enforce the lien is commenced in a court of competent jurisdiction. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 713.22(1))
  • A lien continued beyond 1 year by suing is not enforceable against creditors or subsequent purchasers for value without notice unless a notice of lis pendens is recorded. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 713.22(1))
  • An owner may shorten the time by recording a Notice of Contest of Lien; the lienor must file suit within 60 days after service of the notice or the lien is extinguished automatically. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 713.22(2))
  • A claim of lien may be recorded during the work or thereafter, but not later than 90 days after the final furnishing of labor, services or materials by the lienor. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 713.08(5))

Claim contents and notices

  • The claim of lien must state the lienor's name and address, the person it contracted with, the labor or materials furnished and price, a property description, the owner, the first and last dates furnished, and the unpaid amount. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 713.08(1))
  • Failure to serve a claim of lien under s. 713.18 before recording or within 15 days after recording renders it voidable to the extent of prejudice. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 713.08(4)(c))
  • A lienor not in privity with the owner must serve a notice to owner before commencing, or not later than 45 days after commencing, to furnish labor, services or materials, and in any event before the owner's final payment after the contractor furnishes the final payment affidavit. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 713.06(2)(a))
  • If the owner has properly retained required sums but made improper payments, the owner's property is liable only to the extent of retentions and improper payments. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 713.06)
  • The contractor must give the owner a final payment affidavit stating that all lienors under the direct contract who timely served a notice to owner have been paid, or listing unpaid lienors and amounts. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 713.06(3)(d)1)

What we could not confirm

  • Notice of commencement requirements (s. 713.13) were not opened.
  • Whether a seller's unpaid liens must be paid at closing is a title/closing practice, not confirmed from a statute.

How long does a Florida construction lien last?

One year after recording, unless suit is filed (Sec. 713.22).

What is the claim of lien deadline?

Not later than 90 days after the final furnishing of labor, services or materials (Sec. 713.08).

A Florida condominium association must issue an estoppel certificate within 10 business days of a request, and the fee may not exceed $250 if nothing is owed. A buyer is jointly liable with the previous owner for unpaid assessments that came due before transfer.

Condo estoppel and assessments

  • A condominium association must issue an estoppel certificate within 10 business days after receiving a written or electronic request from a unit owner, designee, mortgagee or mortgagee's designee, and must designate on its website a person or entity with a street or e-mail address for requests. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 718.116(8))
  • A condominium estoppel certificate fee may not exceed $250 if no delinquent amounts are owed; an additional $100 may be charged if delivered on an expedited basis within 3 business days; if delinquent amounts are owed, an additional fee may not exceed $150. Fees adjust every 5 years for CPI. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 718.116(8)(f), (i))
  • A condominium estoppel certificate delivered by hand or electronically is effective for 30 days; sent by regular mail, 35 days. An association waives the right to collect amounts above those stated from a person who in good faith relies on it. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 718.116(8)(b)-(c))
  • If the association fails to deliver within 10 business days, no fee may be charged for the certificate; a summary proceeding under s. 51.011 may compel compliance with prevailing-party attorney fees. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 718.116(8)(d)-(e))
  • A unit owner is jointly and severally liable with the previous owner for all unpaid assessments that came due up to the time of transfer of title. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 718.116(1)(a))

HOA estoppel

  • HOA estoppel: within 10 business days after request from a parcel owner or mortgagee, the association issues the certificate; fee not over $250 (no delinquency), plus $100 expedited (3 business days), plus up to $150 if delinquent; effective 30 days (hand/electronic) or 35 days (mail). (Fla. Stat. Sec. 720.30851(1)-(6))
  • An HOA that fails to deliver the estoppel certificate within 10 business days may not charge a fee; an HOA waives collection of amounts above the certificate from a good-faith relying person. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 720.30851(3)-(4))
  • The estoppel certificate must state whether a capital contribution, resale or transfer fee is due, whether any open rule violation is noticed, whether board approval is required for transfer, and whether a right of first refusal exists. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 720.30851(1))

Reserves and inspections

  • A residential condominium association must have a structural integrity reserve study completed at least every 10 years after the condominium's creation for each building three habitable stories or higher; it covers roof, structure, fireproofing, plumbing, electrical, waterproofing and exterior painting, windows and exterior doors, and other items with deferred maintenance or replacement cost over $25,000 (or inflation-adjusted amount). (Fla. Stat. Sec. 718.112(2)(g))
  • For a budget adopted on or after December 31, 2024, a unit-owner-controlled association required to obtain a SIRS may not provide no reserves or fewer reserves than required for the listed items (multicondominium exception with division-approved alternative funding). (Fla. Stat. Sec. 718.112(2)(g))
  • Milestone inspections apply to buildings three habitable stories or more, are repeated every 10 years, require the association to distribute the inspector's summary to each unit owner within 45 days after receiving the report, and within 180 days after a phase one report the phase two inspector submits a progress report with a timeline. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 553.899)

What we could not confirm

  • The building-age thresholds for milestone inspections.
  • HOA right of first refusal and approval processes not opened beyond estoppel form.
  • Statutory disclosure to buyers of SIRS and milestone reports (s. 718.503) not opened.

10 business days after a written or electronic request (Sec. 718.116(8)).

What can the estoppel fee be?

No more than $250 if no delinquent amounts are owed, with extra charges for expedited delivery, as the statute states.

Who owes unpaid assessments after a sale?

A unit owner is jointly and severally liable with the previous owner for assessments due up to the transfer of title (Sec. 718.116).

When the last borrower on a reverse mortgage dies, the loan becomes due, and HUD gives heirs 30 days to satisfy an FHA-insured HECM, with possible 90-day extensions. This guide uses the HUD heirs flyer and the Florida facts we confirmed.

What we confirmed

  • HUD guidance for inheriting a home with an FHA HECM: the loan must be satisfied within 30 days of the date of the borrower's death; the lender may approve 90-day extensions with documentation that the estate or heirs are actively trying to sell or repay. (HUD, Inheriting a Home Secured by an FHA-insured HECM (Sept. 2019))
  • Heirs may sell the home for at least 95 percent of the current appraised value (the document describes the lender accepting net sale proceeds); if heirs prefer to keep the home, the HECM balance must be paid off in full. (HUD, Inheriting a Home Secured by an FHA-insured HECM)
  • Heirs may transfer title to the lender by deed in lieu of foreclosure to avoid foreclosure. (HUD, Inheriting a Home Secured by an FHA-insured HECM)
  • Documentary stamp tax on a home equity conversion mortgage is computed only on the principal limit available to the borrower, not the maximum claim amount or stated mortgage amount; tax on mortgages is 35 cents per $100. (Fla. Stat. Sec. 201.08(1)(b), (6))
